notes:
I've organised these notes verse by verse. Some limits on what I could cover:

- **Not found:** no Lutheran or Orthodox comment on this chapter, no netbible note for v. 22, and no Bible Odyssey article. I also found no page from my allowed sites that ties Job 21 to prosperity, word-of-faith or hyper-grace teaching by name. I've left all of these out.
- **Unread sources:** I couldn't open Ellicott's full chapter page. The Pulpit Commentary page I read stopped at v. 29.
- **Links for full pages:** Two pages I read in full don't appear in the citation markers: Pulpit Commentary (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/job/21.htm) and Enduring Word (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-21/). For those points I give the URL in brackets.

---

## 1. The traditional reading, verse by verse

**Overview:** Pulpit says Job answers Zophar in one short chapter. Its outline: the wicked are rarely cut off (vv. 17–18); it would be fairer to punish them than their children (vv. 19–21); one fate comes to all (vv. 23–26); popular opinion backs Job (vv. 29–33). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/job/21.htm Guzik says Job won't accept the friends' tidy formula and points out that wicked people often live long, prosperous lives with thriving families and wealth. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-21/

**v. 2:** Pulpit: since the friends have no other comfort to give, they could at least listen carefully. Job will take that as his comfort. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/job/21.htm Matthew Henry adds another reading: listening kindly would be a comfort to the friends themselves later on. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Job/Job_021.cfm

**v. 3:** Pulpit notes the stress on "I" in the Hebrew. Job implies he isn't getting his fair turn, but Pulpit calls this unfair: Job's speeches already fill eleven chapters to the friends' seven. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/job/21.htm Guzik reads "keep mocking" as a sign that neither side has softened and both are speaking sarcastically. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/archives/guzik_david/StudyGuide2017-Job/Job-21.cfm Henry, by contrast, thinks Job hoped a fair hearing would win them over. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Job/Job_021.cfm

**v. 4:** Pulpit: Job isn't bringing his complaint to men but to God, the only one who can really help him. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/job/21.htm If God gives no answer, Job thinks he has a right to be impatient. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/job/21.htm) Guzik: Job's crisis is at heart spiritual, a struggle with God rather than with his friends. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-21/) Gill likewise says the complaint was made to God, not to the friends. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/job-21.html

**v. 5:** Pulpit: "Look at me" means "pay attention." Covering the mouth is an almost universal sign of silence. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/job/21.htm Cambridge (quoted on Bible Hub) calls it a gesture of awed silence, as in Job 40:4. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/job/21-5.htm Henry: the friends should stand in awe of God's hidden ways instead of explaining Job's troubles, and wait without judging. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Job/Job_021.cfm

**v. 6:** Pulpit: Job knows his thesis goes against common religious teaching. He admits he can't think about it without dismay, partly to disarm his critics. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/job/21.htm Henry: what Job remembers is the day he lost everything, compared with how well many wicked people do. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Job/Job_021.cfm

**v. 7:** Guzik: Zophar said the wicked die young (20:4–11); Job says they grow old. If a wicked man can seem blessed, a righteous man can seem cursed. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-21/ Keil & Delitzsch: this directly answers Zophar's claim in 20:5, and the same fact nearly undid Asaph in Psalm 73. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/job/21-7.htm Henry: God lets this happen because it is the day of His patience, but mainly to show that the next world, not this one, is where accounts are settled. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/job/21-7.htm

**v. 8:** Guzik: this answers Bildad's claim (18:19) that the wicked leave no descendants. Job lists exactly the blessings he himself has lost. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-21/

**v. 9:** Pulpit compares Psalm 73:5: God's chastening rod doesn't seem to touch them. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/job/21.htm) Gill: neither the rod of discipline God uses on His own people nor any major judgment falls on them. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/job-21.html

**v. 10:** Pulpit translates "their cow conceives": both conception and birth go well, with no barrenness or miscarriage. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/job/21.htm Henry notes that God promised exactly this to Israel (Exod 23:26; Deut 7:14). https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Job/Job_021.cfm

**vv. 11–12:** Pulpit calls the scene of free, frolicking children "charmingly idyllic." It describes the instruments as tambourine, a simple stringed harp, and a pipe or double reed (not a modern organ). (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/job/21.htm) Henry, more sharply, says the children don't pray or learn the catechism; they dance. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Job/Job_021.cfm

**v. 13:** Pulpit: they die without long illness, unlike Job. Job probably doesn't mean this always happens; he wants the friends to admit there are exceptions to their rule. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/job/21.htm

**v. 14:** Pulpit: it is their freedom from punishment that leads them to reject God; they think they manage fine without Him. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/job/21.htm Clarke (via Guzik): this is what their *conduct* says, though not necessarily their lips. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-21/) Gill: they choose not to know God's ways, so their consciences won't be disturbed. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/job-21.html

**v. 15:** Pulpit compares Pharaoh's "Who is the LORD?" (Exod 5:2) and calls these people agnostics for whom only usefulness counts. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/job/21.htm Gill: prayer stands for all service of God, and the natural man thinks religion gains him nothing (Mal 3:14). https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/job-21.html

**v. 16:** Pulpit: their prosperity isn't their own doing; God's providence is part of it. Yet Job refuses to join them. Satan said Job served God for reward, and here Job keeps clinging to God even if the wicked seem better off. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/job/21.htm Ellicott gives two options. Either it is God who gives them prosperity, which is the mystery; or Job is quoting a reply he expects, then indignantly rejects their reasoning. https://biblehub.com/job/21-16.htm Henry: they didn't gain their wealth without God and can't keep it without Him, so it is ungrateful and foolish to tell Him to leave. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Job/Job_021.cfm

**v. 17:** Pulpit: this is a question, not an exclamation. How often does the wicked man fall? Rarely. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/job/21.htm Gill: God's anger is real, but the sorrows are mostly still in the future. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/job-21.html Henry: you see their candle burn down to the socket as often as you see it snuffed out. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Job/Job_021.cfm

**v. 18:** Pulpit: the "how often" question carries on from v. 17. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/job/21.htm

**v. 19:** Pulpit: Job imagines the friends replying that God punishes the wicked through their children (Exod 20:5). He doesn't deny it, but says God should punish the man himself. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/job/21.htm Andersen (via Guzik) says Job finds the idea monstrous because it invites the thought "we can sin; our children will pay." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-21/)

**v. 20:** Pulpit: being punished himself would bring his guilt home to him far more than suffering through his children. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/job/21.htm Clarke (via Guzik) explains the "cup of wrath" picture (Isa 51; Jer 25; Rev 14). (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-21/) The Geneva Bible note: when God repays him, he will see that his prosperity was empty. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/job/21-20.htm

**v. 21:** Pulpit sums up the wicked man's attitude as "Après moi le déluge" (after me, the flood): what happens to his family after he dies hardly troubles him. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/job/21.htm Gill: once dead, he neither enjoys his children's good fortune nor feels their troubles. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/job-21.html

**v. 22:** Pulpit: Job checks himself, admitting that God's ways can't be searched out. He backs off from claiming a rule (the wicked prosper) to saying no rule can be found. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/job-21.html Guzik: Job half-questions God's wisdom, senses that this is wrong, and corrects himself. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-21/ Henry: dare we tell God which sinner to spare and which to punish? https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Job/Job_021.cfm

**v. 23:** Henry uses the verse as a warning: people die at full strength when they least expect it, so always be ready. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Job/Job_021.cfm

**v. 24:** Pulpit reads "milk-pails" rather than "breasts": in a cattle economy, full pails mean wealth. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/job/21.htm) Poole (via Guzik) says the Hebrew word appears only here, so translations differ. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-21/)

**v. 25:** Pulpit: others suffer bitterly all their lives before they die; "never tasted good." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/job/21.htm)

**v. 26:** Gill: death levels them; they lie in the dust until they are woken at the resurrection. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/job-21.html Poole (via Guzik): no event in this life shows who is good and who is bad. Smick (via Guzik): God would rather we complain than be indifferent. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-21/)

**v. 27:** Pulpit: Job reads between the lines; they suspect him of secret sins. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/job/21.htm) Gill: Job saw from their faces that they weren't persuaded. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/job-21.html

**v. 28:** Pulpit: "the prince's house" is a thinly veiled reference to Job's own fallen household. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/job-21.html

**v. 29:** Barnes: travellers to other lands could have told them the wicked are reserved for later destruction, not hit immediately. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/job/21-29.html Gill gives an unusual reading: travellers could have reported on Job's own character. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/job-21.html

**v. 30:** This is the most debated verse; see sections 2 and 3.

**v. 31:** Constable thinks this is probably Job's own view, not a quotation of the friends. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/job/21-29.html Henry: such a man is one of the "great flies" that break through the law's cobwebs, which only catch the little ones. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Job/Job_021.cfm

**vv. 32–33:** Smick (via Guzik): unlike the friends' picture in chs. 8 and 20, the wicked are often buried with high honours. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-21/) Henry: people say death is the common lot, to soften its shame. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Job/Job_021.cfm

**v. 34:** Pulpit: their comfort is useless because it rests on a false premise, that the godly always prosper. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/job-21.html Henry: where there is no truth, little comfort can be expected. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Job/Job_021.cfm

## 2. Where Protestant traditions differ

The clearest disagreement is at **v. 30**, though it is mainly an interpretive split rather than one that follows denominational lines.

- **Reformed:**
  - Gill: the wicked are spared now but reserved, by God's decree, for eternal destruction. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/job/21-30.html
  - Geneva Bible: though the wicked flourish, God will punish them at the last day. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/job/21-30.htm
  - Henry: Job was clearly right that the wicked's destruction is reserved for the next world. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Job/Job_021.cfm
- **Methodist / Wesleyan:** Wesley thinks the switch to the plural hints that only some are punished now, but all will be then. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/job/21-30.html Clarke: prosperity is no proof of God's love; the "day of wrath" comes in the next world. https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/lsv/job/21-30.html Benson argues that a merely earthly destruction would prove the friends right, so it must mean final judgment. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/job/21-30.html
- **Baptist:** Spurgeon preached this verse as describing final judgment and the resurrection of the body. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/job/21-30.html
- **Calvary Chapel / Pentecostal-leaning:** Chuck Smith: God will judge them, but not necessarily in this life. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/job/21-30.html Guzik: Job's frustration is that judgment doesn't come fast enough. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-21/)
- **The opposite reading, "spared *in*" the day of disaster:**
  - Pulpit (non-denominational) and Ellicott: the wicked are spared *in* the day of destruction, i.e. they escape it. https://biblehub.com/job/21-30.htm
  - Cambridge: they are led away to safety. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/job/21-30.htm
  - Barnes reports Rosenmüller and others holding "spared." He himself prefers "reserved for," judging from the Hebrew. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/job/21-30.html

**v. 23:** Gill notes some apply it to a good man dying in peace through Christ. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/job-21.html

**v. 27:** Gill draws a Christ-centred point: only God truly knows thoughts, so Christ's knowing them shows He is God. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/job-21.html

## 3. Other views

**Modern scholarship (NET notes)**, all at https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Job&chapter=21:
- **v. 2:** the Greek Old Testament (LXX) turns the line into a negative. https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Job&chapter=21
- **v. 3:** "mock" is singular, so Job may be addressing Zophar alone. https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Job&chapter=21
- **v. 4:** following Rowley: complaints against men might win sympathy, but nobody dares sympathise with a complaint against God. https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Job&chapter=21
- **v. 10:** the rabbinic reading is "does not fail to breed." https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Job&chapter=21
- **v. 13:** the key word may mean "in a moment" or "in peace"; Gordis thinks both meanings are meant. https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Job&chapter=21
- **v. 17:** "pangs," as in birth pains. https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Job&chapter=21
- **v. 19:** "They say" is supplied by translators, as an idea Job suspects the friends hold. https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Job&chapter=21
- **v. 30:** "led forth" in the day of trouble means delivered. https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Job&chapter=21
- **v. 31:** the questions expect the answer "No one!" https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Job&chapter=21

**Layman's Bible Commentary** (v. 16): it takes the opposite view from the traditional commentators. To the wicked, their prosperity is "in their own hand" and not from God. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/lbc/job-21.html

**Catholic:**
- **v. 30:** Haydock offers two readings: he is repaid at last, or God protects him while others are in danger. He cites the LXX/Theodotion reading "kept on high." https://www.studylight.org/commentary/job/21-30.html
- **v. 16:** the Douay-Rheims reads it as a prayer, "may the counsel of the wicked be far from me." https://biblehub.com/job/21-16.htm

**Prosperity-related themes:** I found no source on these sites that names prosperity, word-of-faith or hyper-grace teaching in connection with this chapter. The nearest points:
- Chuck Smith calls the friends' idea, that prosperity proves righteousness and calamity proves wickedness, a basic fallacious philosophy. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/job/21-7.html
- Pulpit's Adeney homily: prosperity isn't the highest good; true prosperity is prosperity of the soul. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/job-21.html
